qdg9n1:288: GenRec is an LLM-backed recommender ranker built by Netflix: starting from an internal foundation LLM, it performs post-training on Netflix-specific data, verbalizes user history, item metadata, and context in natural language, and uses a catalog-aware scoring head to score and rank items across the entire catalog. saud9y:225: GenRec uses two-stage training: Phase 1 starts from an open-source LLM and adapts it on Netflix-specific corpora into a "Netflix-aware" foundation model (content understanding, member behavior preference patterns, general language ability), updated infrequently and shared as a backbone across multiple applications; Phase 2 performs post-training on ranking-specific data and objectives, focusing on ranking quality and steering, incorporating multiple reward signals, updated more frequently to track new content and taste drift, and explicitly optimized under serving-cost constraints.
ukrm9x:260: GenRec is trained jointly with multi-objective losses: ① catalog-aware ranking objective (higher scores for positive samples given the verbalized context, cross-entropy loss); ② language modeling objective (preserves general language understanding and leaves the door open for text generation such as recommendation explanations); ③ reward-weighted alignment — an independent reward model provides signals used to weight each training sample (long-term satisfaction proxy + behavior rebalancing, e.g., games vs. movies, new titles vs. long-tail), giving high-value interactions more weight and low-value ones less. The reward-weighted approach is simpler and cheaper than full RL; in practice RL methods like GRPO add further gains but at higher cost, left as future work.

yn6w2m:253: Traditional recommenders rely on dense features and embeddings; GenRec verbalizes user history and context into natural language and encodes it directly into the LLM's semantic space, letting the model discover item relationships and interest evolution on its own. The context window becomes the new "feature budget", which motivates context engineering: fully retaining high-signal interactions (long plays, likes), omitting low-signal events (very short plays, quick hovers), compressing repetitive behaviors (binge-watching), selectively expanding cold-start or important items; within a fixed token budget, prioritize recent high-signal history and maximize shared prefixes to benefit from prefix caching.
